title: Two Indians Among 28 Green Card Holders Charged in California Voting Case
excerpt: Amandeep Kaur of Rancho Palos Verdes and Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah of Sacramento are among 28 lawful permanent residents charged in the Justice Department's Operation Protect the Vote. Eleven were arrested Monday; all are presumed innocent.
body:
• Federal authorities have charged 28 green card holders across California in "Operation Protect the Vote"; 11 were arrested on Monday, October 19, according to the Justice Department.
  • Two defendants are Indian nationals: Amandeep Kaur, 30, of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, of Sacramento, both accused of registering and voting in the November 2024 election.
  • Charges include fraudulent voter registration and false statements in a naturalization application, felonies carrying up to five years in federal prison; the Eastern District voting-by-an-alien charge is a misdemeanor carrying up to one year.
  • What this means for you: green card holders may not register or vote in U.S. elections at any level. Doing so — or claiming U.S. citizenship on any form — can bring felony charges and destroy a pending naturalization case. All defendants are presumed innocent.

Federal law enforcement arrested 11 foreign nationals across California on Monday and charged 28 in total with election crimes, the U.S. Department of Justice announced, in a coordinated sweep it calls "Operation Protect the Vote." All 28 defendants are lawful permanent residents — green card holders — who, the department said, fraudulently registered to vote in U.S. elections and in most cases cast ballots. Two of the 28 are Indian nationals.

Amandeep Kaur, 30, an Indian national living in Rancho Palos Verdes who is seeking to become a U.S. citizen, is accused of fraudulently registering to vote in December 2022 and voting in the November 2024 U.S. election, according to the Justice Department's announcement. Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, an Indian national living in Sacramento, is accused of registering on the day of the November 2024 general election and voting that day; he is charged by information in the Eastern District of California. Both cases are allegations. The department notes that a complaint, indictment and information "merely contain accusations" and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

What the complaints allege

According to court documents cited by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California, the defendants "knowingly and willfully lied under oath in their voter registration applications that they were U.S. citizens." Their registrations were approved, many of them voted, and prosecutors allege that several later lied again in naturalization paperwork by stating they had never claimed U.S. citizenship and had never registered or voted. The operation spans all four California U.S. Attorney's offices. In the Central District, defendants face felony charges including false statements in a naturalization application; in the Eastern District, including Shah's case, the charge is voting by an alien in a federal election, a misdemeanor carrying a maximum of one year. The felony charges carry a statutory maximum of five years in federal prison.

"Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen."

— Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Attorney General

The arrests follow a direct clash with the state. On October 13, the federal government gave California a list of the 28 individuals so their vote-by-mail ballots could be set aside while citizenship was confirmed. California declined to help, and the United States sued, seeking a court order on ballot counting. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said each defendant appears on a larger list of more than 20,000 "likely noncitizen registrants" provided to California election officials last week. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said nationwide the Justice Department has now charged 113 people with illegal voting and registration offenses, USA Today reported.

California's response

State officials dispute the federal methodology. Secretary of State Shirley Weber said she will not disenfranchise thousands of Californians based on an "unsupported" and "likely inaccurate" belief, noting ballots are delivered and voting is underway, according to USA Today. Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said his office "cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations." The 28 defendants, however, are named in individual criminal complaints, not only on the larger list.

Why this matters for green card holders

This case is distinct from the single-defendant Minnesota prosecution The Videshi covered earlier this month: it is a statewide, multi-district operation built around a 20,000-name registrant list, arriving weeks before the midterms with early voting underway. For the Indian community, the lesson is stark: permanent residents have legal status, but voting rights belong only to citizens. Registering — even on a form someone else hands you — and then denying it on a naturalization application compounds a registration problem into an alleged false-statement felony. Anyone who may have registered in error should get immigration counsel before filing any application.

The defendants arrested Monday were expected to make initial appearances in U.S. District Court the same afternoon, with no pleas taken. Authorities said the remaining charged individuals would be taken into custody or summoned in the near future.
